questions.q: What is the key difference between a C array and a C struct?
choices: An array is an ordered collection of elements of the same type; a struct groups data elements that can have different types
An array can hold only numbers; a struct can hold only strings
Arrays are stored in memory; structs exist only at compile time
A struct is an ordered collection of elements of the same type; an array groups elements of different types
questions.explain: Arrays hold elements of the same type, in order. Structs hold a heterogeneous collection of data, such as a char array, an int and a float, and treat it as a single unit.

questions.q: C supports classes, and `struct` is the keyword C uses to define one.
questions.explain: C is not an object-oriented language and has no classes. A struct is like the data part of a class: it groups fields but has no methods.

questions.q: What is the correct order of steps for defining and using a struct type in a C program?
choices: Declare variables of the struct type, define the struct type, access fields with dot notation
Define the struct type, declare variables of that type, access individual fields with dot notation
Define the struct type, access fields with dot notation, declare variables of that type
Access fields with dot notation, declare variables, define the struct type
questions.explain: First define the new struct type, then declare variables of that type, then use dot (.) notation to read or set each variable's fields.

questions.q: Where should a struct type definition normally appear in a .c file?
choices: Inside main, just before the variables that use it
Outside of any function, typically near the top of the file
Inside every function that uses the struct
Inside a comment block so the compiler can find it
questions.explain: A struct type definition should appear outside of any function, usually near the top of the .c file, so the whole program can use the type.
The new type's name is two words: `struct studentT`. Types like int, char and float are a single word, but a struct type's name includes the `struct` keyword.

questions.q: Assume `struct studentT` has already been defined and no typedef is used. Which line correctly declares two variables of that type?
choices: `studentT student1, student2;`
`struct studentT student1, student2;`
`struct student1, student2;`
`struct studentT {student1, student2};`
questions.explain: The type name is `struct studentT`, so a declaration looks like `struct studentT student1, student2;`.

questions.q: Which struct type definition has correct syntax?
choices: `struct point { int x; int y; };`
`struct point { int x; int y; }`
`struct point { int x, int y };`
`struct point ( int x; int y; );`
questions.explain: The general form is `struct <name> { <type> <field>; ... };`. Fields go in braces, each one ends with a semicolon, and the closing brace is followed by a semicolon.

questions.q: `student1` is a `struct studentT` whose `name` field is declared as `char name[64];`. What is the C type of the expression `student1.name[3]`?
choices: `struct studentT`
`char []` (array of characters)
`char`
`int`
questions.explain: `student1.name` is a char array, so indexing into it with `[3]` gives one character, of type `char`.

questions.q: `student1` is a `struct studentT` whose `name` field is declared as `char name[64];`. What is the C type of the expression `student1.name`?
choices: `struct studentT`
`char []` (array of characters)
`char`
`int`
questions.explain: The `name` field is a character array. `student1` itself has type `struct studentT`, and one element such as `student1.name[3]` is a `char`.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: to access the `age` field of a struct variable named `student1`, you write `student1___age`. What symbol goes in the blank?
questions.explain: Fields are accessed with dot notation: `<variable name>.<field name>`, for example `student1.age`.

questions.q: `student1`'s `name` field is declared as `char name[64];`. Which statement correctly stores the string "Kwame Salter" in that field?
choices: `student1.name = "Kwame Salter";`
`strcpy(student1.name, "Kwame Salter");`
`student1.name[] = "Kwame Salter";`
`strcpy("Kwame Salter", student1.name);`
questions.explain: `name` is a statically declared char array, so it can't be the target of `=`. Use `strcpy` with the destination first to copy the string's characters into the array.

questions.q: printf has a format placeholder that prints a whole `struct studentT` variable in one go.
questions.explain: printf has no placeholder for a programmer-defined struct type. Pass each field separately, for example `%s` for name, `%d` for age, `%g` for gpa and `%d` for grad_yr.

choices: `student1.age = 18;`
`arr = "hello";`
`student2 = student1;`
`student1.name = student2.name;`
`arr[3] = ch;`
questions.explain: Single variables of base types, array elements, struct fields of base types and whole structs are lvalues. `x + 1` is not an lvalue. A statically declared array name (`arr`, `student1.name`) is not an lvalue because its base address can't be changed. Use strcpy to copy strings into it instead.

questions.q: What is the term for an expression that can appear on the left side of an assignment statement because it represents a memory storage location?
questions.explain: An lvalue represents a memory storage location, so it can be assigned to. Struct variables are lvalues, which is why `student2 = student1;` is valid.

questions.q: `student1` and `student2` are both `struct studentT` variables. What happens when `student2 = student1;` runs?
choices: It is a compile error because structs must be copied field by field
student2 becomes another name for the same memory as student1
The contents of student1's memory (every field value, including every character of the name array) are copied into student2's memory
Only the non-array fields are copied, so name must be copied separately with strcpy
questions.explain: Struct variables are lvalues, and a struct's value is the contents of its memory. Assigning one struct to another copies every field value into the other struct's own memory. The two variables stay separate.

choices: student1.name is "Kwame Salter"; student2.name is "Frances Allen"
Both are "Frances Allen"
Both are "Kwame Salter"
student1.name is "Frances Allen"; student2.name is "Kwame Salter"
questions.explain: `student2 = student1;` copies student1's field values into student2's separate memory. The later strcpy changes only student2's name array, so student1 still holds "Kwame Salter".
The struct assignment copies all of student1's fields, including age (20), into student2. Only grad_yr is changed afterward (to 2021), so student2.age is still 20.

questions.q: `name` is declared as `char name[64];` inside `struct studentT`. Why is `student1.name = student2.name;` invalid C?
choices: `name` is a statically declared array, so it is not an lvalue: its base address can't be changed (use strcpy instead)
Struct fields can never appear on the left side of an assignment
Two different struct variables can't share any field names
The `name` fields become read-only once the struct variables are declared
questions.explain: Fields of base types such as `student1.age` are lvalues, but the name of a statically declared array is not. Copying a string into the array needs `strcpy(student1.name, student2.name);`. Assigning the whole struct (`student1 = student2;`) is also valid.
64 bytes for the name array, 4 for age, 4 for gpa and 4 for grad_yr: 64 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 76.

questions.q: `sizeof(struct studentT)` (fields: `char name[64]`, `int age`, `float gpa`, `int grad_yr`) is always exactly 76 bytes on every machine.
questions.explain: It is at least 76 bytes, the sum of the field sizes, but on some machines the exact number can be larger.
To reach gpa, the compiler skips the 64-character name array and one int (age): 64 + 4 = 68.

questions.q: A struct variable's field names (such as "age" and "gpa") are stored in memory next to the field values.
questions.explain: Only the field values are stored. To the compiler, a field is just a storage location at a known offset from the start of the struct's memory.

questions.q: In C, how is a struct argument passed to a function's struct parameter?
choices: By value: the parameter gets a copy of all the argument's field values
By reference: the parameter shares the argument's memory
Only the struct's starting address is passed
Only the fields that the function actually uses are copied
questions.explain: In C, arguments of every type are passed by value. A struct's value is its whole memory contents, so the parameter gets its own copy of every field.

choices: Ruth is 19 years old / Ruth is only 17 years old and cannot vote.
Ruth is 19 years old / Ruth is only 19 years old and cannot vote.
Ruth is 17 years old / Ruth is only 17 years old and cannot vote.
Ruth is 19 years old / Ruth is 19 years old and can vote.

birthday receives a copy of student1. Incrementing the parameter's age changes only the copy, so student1.age is still 20 in main.

questions.q: A struct has a statically declared array field (`char name[64]`) and is passed to a function. The function then changes the parameter's array contents, for example with `strcpy(s.name, "X")`. After the function returns, the caller's struct shows the change.
questions.explain: When a struct is passed, its entire memory contents, including every element of an array field, are copied into the parameter. Changes to the parameter's array affect only that copy and don't persist after the function returns.
